title: Order Books
summary: An order book stores bids and asks by price level and matches incoming orders by defined rules (price-time, pro-rata, etc.). Structure choice (trees, arrays of levels, intrusive lists) drives latency and determinism.

sections.title: Book mechanics
paragraphs: Limit orders rest; market orders aggress. Price-time priority is common: better price first, then earlier time. Partial fills and cancel/replace are first-class.

sections.title: Data structures
paragraphs: Price levels often in sorted maps or contiguous arrays for hot top-of-book. Orders in FIFO queues per level. Avoid allocations on the hot path — preallocate pools.

sections.title: Determinism and journaling
paragraphs: For audit and replay, apply a sequenced input log to a deterministic book. Same inputs → same trades. This is the backbone of exchange reliability.

sections.title: Market data
paragraphs: Publishing top-of-book vs full depth changes bandwidth. Conflate wisely; never block matching on slow consumers.

deepDive.title: Order Books — Operations
paragraphs: Operating Order Books in production means defining SLIs before tuning knobs, knowing amplification costs, and rehearsing failure modes.
Prefer reversible changes, feature flags, and canaries. Measure p50/p99 and error rate under load that matches production skew.
bullets: Define capacity from the scarcest resource
Keep rollback cheaper than forward repair when possible

deepDive.title: Order Books — Failure modes
paragraphs: Common failures around Order Books include overload, partial dependency outages, and silent correctness bugs that pass happy-path tests.
Inject faults in staging: latency, loss, clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts fire and degradation is intentional.

expert.title: Order Books — Expert notes
paragraphs: At the expert level, Order Books intersects multi-region consistency, cost envelopes, and organizational constraints (team ownership, on-call load).
Write down the non-goals. Many outages come from optimizing a metric that was never the product requirement.

pitfalls: Allocating per order in steady state
keyTakeaways: Books are specialized deterministic state machines
Latency and fairness rules dominate structure choice
whyItMatters: Trading and other continuous double-auction markets require this pattern; it also teaches extreme low-latency design.
reflectionQuestions: How would you prove two implementations produce identical matches?
numbersToKnow: Know your p99 latency budget before adding hops
Peak load ≠ average load — plan headroom (often 2–3×)
Cross-region RTT is often ~50–150ms one way
